Obtemperatum sine mora, itumque Lugdunum Batavorum Aprili mense; brevi autem mutato consilio in agrum Leodiensem digressi prope castrum quoddam confederunt, ubi mox se minus tutos rati, urbem ipsam ingressi sunt, feque ibidem ad finem usque Augusti paucissimis consciis continuerunt; quando jactationem exosi contemto periculo Bruxellas iterum post semestre spatium furtim reversi, antiquas latebras petierunt, e quibus teste Quesnello ipso in suis quibusdam literis toto quadriennio, quo Arnaldus supervixerat, pedem non extulerunt. Hoc tempore Quesnellus opus suum perpolivit, Arnaldus eo adminiculante extremas vires suas contra Bullas Pontificum, & contra recens Decretum Alexandri VIII, quo 31. propositiones, pluresque Arnaldinæ damnata sunt, in libro *difficultates propositæ contra Steyartum Doctorem Lovaniensem* scripto experiri voluit, quo perfunctus labore fenex depontanus 82. annorum accepto e Quesnelli manibus viatico 8. Augusti 1694. exspiravit.

However, having changed their plan shortly after, they departed into the territory of Liège and settled near a certain castle. There, soon considering themselves less safe, they entered the city itself and kept themselves there until the end of August with very few aware of their presence. When they grew weary of wandering, they disregarded the danger and furtively returned to Brussels after a six-month interval, seeking their old hiding places, from which, according to Quesnel himself in some of his letters, they did not step foot for the entire four years that Arnauld survived. At this time, Quesnel polished his work, and Arnauld, with him assisting, wished to exert his remaining strength against the Bulls of the Pontiffs and against the recent Decree of Alexander VIII—by which 31 propositions and several of Arnauld’s were condemned—in a book written as *Difficulties proposed against Steyaert, a Doctor of Louvain*. Having finished this labor, the 82-year-old man, deprived of his censorship, expired on August 8, 1694, having received the viaticum from the hands of Quesnel.

107. But Christ teaches us otherwise: that it is hidden from the clever and wise, and manifest to the simple, the seeking, and the hungry. As Mary also says: "He casts the mighty from their thrones and exalts the wretched and lowly, who are humble in their hearts before Him, not by my power and might, but by Spirit and strength."

Noailles was further terrified by the Council of Embrun and by the King's authority in defending its acts. In 1727, several bishops had gathered at Embrun to defeat the monstrous errors that were being scattered everywhere by the schismatics and to settle the disturbances they had incited. Furthermore, there were two primary acts: the condemnation of Father Courrayer, from the monastery of Saint Genevieve, along with his book against the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist, who set out for England to carry out the system of Dupin and distinguished himself there with other writings regarding the ordinations of Anglican bishops; and second, the sentence passed on September 20th against Soanen, the Bishop of Senez. A certain pastoral Instruction had appeared under his name, teeming with infamous errors of every kind, and in which, as much as Quesnel’s work was commended, the Bull condemning it was prostituted as worthy of all execration. It is con-

demned by the bishops; he himself was summoned to the council to give an account. Soanen initially prevaricated, naming thirteen bishops before whom he would plead his case, and against whom he himself had nothing to object; finally, he set out for Embrun, not without an irreverent retinue, and not unarmed. But before he entered the city, he ordered it to be announced to those gathered that he would never recognize them as judges. Then, when asked by the Council whether that was his Instruction, he indeed denied that it had been drafted by him; nevertheless, he openly professed that he entirely adopted, held, and approved of it as his own, until he could be convinced of the errors the bishops had condemned in it. In truth, the stubbornness of this man could not be overcome. Therefore, by the sentence of the Council, he was forbidden from all functions, both Episcopal and Priestly, and a Vicar General was appointed for his diocese. It would be tedious to recount the outcries and tumults that this scene produced. Twelve bishops protested against this sentence and delivered a protest to the King himself. …and should announce to you from the word of God that doctrine which Osiander [treats] as not sufficiently sincere, and others—his associates—even anathematize as erroneous, I cannot, Brothers, unless I wish to be deemed a plain impostor and pseudoprophetēs , fail to defend with all my might that for which I am prepared to pour out my life itself, if the Lord so wills. When, therefore, we see that an account of our faith is demanded, it must certainly be rendered according to the precept of Peter. For he conducts this cause so astutely that, while attributing great praises—both of singular piety toward God and of patience—to you (that is, the flock and little sheep, as he calls them), he ascribes the whole blame for the errors (in which, if it pleases God, he wishes the Gallic and reformed Churches of Christ to be entangled) to us, the Pastors. Thus he tries to tear us Pastors away from you, the sheep, and you, the sheep, away from us, the Pastors—that is, the most closely joined members of the same body—so that, just as he scattered those fatal discords in the midst of Germany, he might also be able to disseminate the same dissensions in the Gallic Churches on account of Ubiquity.*

# AD ECCLES. GALLIC.

Osiander, so that you may know the man, is the diapyros and carrier of a certain new Pandora, manufactured by—I know not whom—Vulcan, which he has undertaken to carry off to other shores and provinces of the world, such as Gaul and Belgium. But he either thinks you are logs and stumps, to tolerate such bitter [charges] for so long, concerning a doctrine unknown to you and never weighed against the standard of the Divine word as a just scale; or, if he thinks you are pious and prudent, he ought surely to have thought well of you, and to have assumed that you had done what is written of the Beroeans and Thessalonians, namely, that you would search the scriptures and diligently compare our doctrine with them. That, however, brothers, you have done and are doing, by the grace of God, and because of this you are confirmed more and more each day by the spirit of God in that doctrine which you have received from us. Furthermore, when this man so proudly condemns all the Pastors of the Gallic Churches together in one judgment, as if they were whitewashed walls, how many and how great—immortal God—men does he condemn? …grandes Böhmii illius. Quid dicam? ut legi, ut obstupui. Itáne virum è multis, in schola non eruditum, tàm profunda mysteria aggredi, & tàm politè scribere! Enimverò ipsa methodus, & rer. abditar. expositio facit, ut dubitem de autore. Dicitur esse idiota Böhmius. Nondum credere possumus nisi certior adhuc fiam, talem esse Görlitii, talia eum scripsisse: idque unius & alterius viri sincerioris testimonio, &c. Unter erwehnten des J.B. gewesenen Freunden war sonderlich einer/dessen Beywohnung ich offt und viel genossen/ welcher zu erzhelen wuste/wie ein Med. Doctor allhie/ Tob. Kober genandt/den ich noch wohl gekennet/ den J.B. mit seiner Natur-Sprache zu mehrmalen auf die Probe gefeset/in dem sie/als geheime Freunde/im Spaziergehen/einer dem andern Blumen/ Kräuter/und andere Erdgewächse zeiget/un J.B. aus deren eusserlichen Signatur und Bildung/ die innerliche Krafft/ Würckung und Eigenschafften/ mit denen Buchstaben/Syllaben und Worten des ihnen eingesprochenen und zugegebenen Namens alsobald beudet. I cannot believe it yet, unless I am made more certain that such a person exists in Görlitz and that he has written such things; and this by the testimony of one or another more sincere man, etc. Among the aforementioned friends of J.B. whom I have known, there was one in particular, whose company I often and much enjoyed, who knew how to tell how a medical doctor here, named Tob. Kober—whom I also knew well—put J.B. to the test several times with his language of nature, in that they, as secret friends, would show each other flowers, herbs, and other plants of the earth while walking, and J.B. would immediately indicate the inner power, effect, and properties from their outward signatura and formation, together with the letters, syllables, and words of the name spoken into and attributed to them. However, he wanted to hear the names, above others, in the Hebrew language, as it would be the closest to the language of nature; and when one did not know those same names, he asked after the Greek
